title: Entering the stream
hookLine: at the first stage three fetters fall: self-view, doubt, clinging to rites
last: FOUR STAGES — A MAP, NOT A SCOREBOARD.

cards: In the Buddha's city of Savatthi, a great supporter of the monks, a merchant named Anathapindika, had a son named Kala who wanted nothing to do with any of it.
So his father made the offer parents still make: I'll pay you. Keep the observance day, go hear the Buddha, and there's a hundred coins in it for you. Kala went, for the money.
He went again. The story says the Buddha made sure the teaching kept him listening a little longer each time. And then something happened that no amount of money had planned for.

teach.b: Kala became a sotāpanna. Sota, the stream. Āpanna, entered. A stream-enterer.
When he came home, his father set out a thousand coins, and Kala didn't want them.

The commentary tells this story behind a verse of the Dhammapada, which Max Müller renders: "Better than sovereignty over the earth, better than going to heaven, better than lordship over all worlds, is the reward of the first step in holiness."
What is that first step? The suttas say three fetters fall.
First, self-view: the belief in a fixed, permanent me at the center of everything. The stream-enterer doesn't forget their name; the old conviction of a solid self is seen through.
Second, doubt: not ordinary questions, but the gnawing uncertainty about whether the path leads anywhere. The stream-enterer has seen enough to know.
Third, clinging to rites and rules: the belief that ceremonies or vows, all by themselves, can purify you. This one surprises people. Stream-enterers still chant, bow and keep precepts.
What drops is treating the ritual as a magic switch.

In another sutta the Buddha names four marks of a stream-enterer: unshakable trust in the Buddha, the teaching and the community, and a life of good conduct that the wise would praise. The image is a river.

teach.h: IN THE CURRENT, TOWARD THE SEA.
teach.b: Once you're in the current, it carries you toward the sea. You can still swim slowly, but you won't be washed back up the bank. The texts say at most seven more lives.
Kala entered the stream because he was paid to listen. Some doors open that way.

how: Theravada Buddhists regard stream-entry as the first real turning point on the path; lay people as well as monks are said to attain it, and the four factors of stream-entry are taught in sermons and study.

o: a monk who has kept the precepts for a year
one who has entered the stream toward awakening
a new member who has just joined a temple group

games.q: match each piece of today's teaching.
p: paid to go hear the Buddha
belief in a fixed, permanent me

s: they keep practices; what drops is treating ritual as a magic switch.
the texts say a stream-enterer has at most seven more lives
once in the current, they won't be washed back up the bank.
he no longer wanted them; the verse calls the first step better than lordship over all worlds.

games.q: you're Kala. you went to hear the Buddha for the money, and something changed. now your father offers you a thousand coins. what do you do, as the story tells it?
o: take them; a deal is a deal.
decline them; you've found something better.
games.why: Kala didn't want the coins, and the Dhammapada verse says the reward of the first step is better than any sovereignty or heaven.

practice: Bring to mind one ritual you hold onto: a lucky shirt, a routine you're sure the day will fall apart without, the phone checked the moment you wake.
No need to drop it; look at it kindly and ask, what am I trusting this to do for me? Then let the question go, and picture yourself stepping into a river's current, feeling it gently carry you.

wordCard.voice: Sotapanna. A stream-enterer: the first of the four stages, when self-view, doubt and clinging to rites fall away.

orig.note: Pali sotāpanna: sota (stream) + āpanna (entered), a stream-enterer.

carryVoice: Your line: some doors open that way. Even one opened for a hundred coins. On to day three hundred.
